notes.heading: Covalent bonds and the octet rule
points: A covalent bond is the electrostatic attraction between a shared electron pair and the two positively charged nuclei.
Covalent bonding is likely when electronegativity difference is small (below about 1.8) and both atoms are non-metals.
Octet rule: atoms tend to reach 8 valence electrons. Exceptions: electron-deficient species (BF3, BeCl2, AlCl3), odd-electron species, expanded octets.
Lewis formula shows only valence electrons, in pairs: bonding pairs between atoms, lone pairs away from the bond region.
Steps: count valence electrons (add for negative charge, subtract for positive), halve to get pairs, single bonds, fill outer atoms, rest on centre, make multiple bonds if needed.

notes.heading: Single, double and triple bonds
points: Single, double, triple bonds share one, two, three pairs; bond order is 1, 2, 3.
Greater bond order means a stronger bond (larger bond enthalpy) and a shorter bond length.
C–C: 346 kJ mol⁻¹, 154 pm; C=C: 614, 134 pm; C≡C: 839, 120 pm (units: 10⁻¹² m).
Bond length is the average distance between two bonded nuclei.

notes.heading: Coordination bonds
points: In a coordination bond both bonding electrons come from one atom; the arrow points from donor to acceptor.
Examples: H₃O⁺ (H⁺ accepts a lone pair from water), NH₄⁺, CO, NH₃→BF₃.
Once formed, it is indistinguishable from any other covalent bond.
AHL: transition metal complexes such as [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ have ligands donating lone pairs to the central metal cation.

notes.heading: VSEPR and molecular shapes
points: Electron domains (lone pair, single bond, or a whole double/triple bond) repel and spread as far apart as possible.
Lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, and multiple bonds more than single bonds, so bond angles shrink or deviate.
2 domains linear 180°; 3 domains trigonal planar 120° (bent <120° with 1 lone pair); 4 domains tetrahedral 109.5°.
With 4 domains: 1 lone pair gives trigonal pyramidal (NH₃ 107°); 2 lone pairs gives bent (H₂O 104.5°).
Method: count domains for the electron domain geometry, then count bonding and non-bonding domains for molecular geometry.

notes.heading: Bond polarity
points: Bond polarity comes from the electronegativity difference; the shared pair shifts towards the more electronegative atom.
That atom gets δ–, the other δ+. A larger difference means a more polar bond.
A dipole can be drawn as a vector arrow pointing to the more electronegative atom, starting with a plus sign.
Identical atoms (F₂, Br₂) share equally: pure covalent, non-polar, no dipole.

notes.heading: Molecular polarity
points: Molecular polarity depends on both bond polarity and molecular geometry; dipole moment unit is the debye, D.
Polar if bond dipoles do not cancel, giving a net dipole (H₂O, CHCl₃).
Non-polar if polar bond dipoles cancel by symmetry (BF₃, CO₂), or if bonds are non-polar or nearly so (hydrocarbons like ethane).
Always link the shape to the cancelling or non-cancelling of dipoles in an explanation.

notes.heading: Covalent network structures
points: Network structures are continuous 3D lattices of covalent bonds (diamond, graphite, SiO₂, Si), unlike discrete molecules.
Diamond: each C bonded to 4, tetrahedral; very hard, no mobile charges so poor electrical conductor.
Graphite: each C bonded to 3, trigonal planar layers; delocalized electrons conduct; weak London forces between layers make it slippery.
Graphene is a single graphite layer; C₆₀ is molecular, with weak intermolecular forces and a low boiling point.
Allotropes differ in structure and so in properties. SiO₂ has Si:O 1:2, each Si bonded to four O; hard, high melting point.

notes.heading: Types of intermolecular forces
points: Intermolecular forces are weak electrostatic attractions between molecules; they are overcome on melting or boiling, not the covalent bonds.
London (dispersion) forces: all molecules, from temporary induced dipoles; stronger with more electrons and a larger contact area.
Dipole–dipole between polar molecules; dipole–induced dipole between a polar and a non-polar molecule.
Hydrogen bond: H bonded to N, O or F attracts a lone pair on another N, O or F atom.
Van der Waals forces collectively: London, dipole–induced dipole and dipole–dipole.

notes.heading: Strength and properties of covalent substances
points: With comparable molar mass: London < dipole–dipole < hydrogen bonding; dipole–induced dipole sits between London and dipole–dipole.
Typical enthalpies, kJ mol⁻¹: London 1–5, dipole–dipole 3–25, hydrogen bond 20–40; covalent bonds are 150–600.
Network solids: non-volatile, insoluble, poor conductors (except graphite/graphene). Molecular: volatile, poor conductors, varied solubility.
Like dissolves like: polar solutes in polar solvents; molecules able to hydrogen bond with water dissolve; long hydrocarbon chains do not.

notes.heading: Chromatography and RF values
points: Chromatography separates by different attraction (intermolecular forces) to the mobile phase and the stationary phase.
Components with greater affinity for the mobile phase travel further.
RF = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent front; no unit, always between 0 and 1.
Paper: polar water-rich cellulose stationary phase. TLC: polar silica/alumina; polar components move less, non-polar move further.
RF values identify substances only if conditions (solvent, temperature, etc.) are the same.

notes.heading: Resonance and delocalization
points: Resonance structures are used when a double bond could be drawn in more than one position; shown with a double-headed arrow.
The real molecule is a hybrid, not flipping between structures.
Delocalization: electrons shared across more than two atoms, giving equal bonds of intermediate length, strength and order.
Ozone and NO₂⁻ have bond order 1.5; carbonate has 1.33.

notes.heading: Benzene
points: Benzene C₆H₆: planar ring of six carbons with delocalized electrons, drawn as two resonance structures or a circle.
Physical evidence: all C–C bonds are 140 pm, between single (154) and double (134), with intermediate strength.
Chemical evidence: it undergoes substitution rather than addition, since addition would destroy the stabilizing delocalized ring.
Resonance energy is 152 kJ mol⁻¹: predicted cyclohexatriene hydrogenation 360 versus actual 208 kJ mol⁻¹.
Only one 1,2-dichlorobenzene isomer exists because all carbons are equivalent.

notes.heading: Expanded octets
points: Larger central atoms can have 5 or 6 electron pairs (10 or 12 electrons), e.g. PF₅, SF₆, ICl₄⁻.
Draw as normal but skip the final check that the central atom has an octet.
5 domains trigonal bipyramidal: 0 lone pairs trigonal bipyramidal (PF₅), 1 seesaw (SF₄), 2 T-shaped (ClF₃), 3 linear (I₃⁻).
6 domains octahedral: 0 lone pairs octahedral (SF₆), 1 square pyramidal (BrF₅), 2 square planar (XeF₄).
Angles: 90° and 120° (trigonal bipyramidal), 90° (octahedral); lone pairs reduce them.

notes.heading: Formal charge
points: FC = VE – (NBE + ½BE), where NBE is non-bonding electrons and BE is bonding electrons on the atom.
Formal charges must sum to the overall charge of the species.
Preferred Lewis formula: formal charges closest to zero, smallest differences, negative charge on the more electronegative atom.
Example: SO₄²⁻ with expanded octet sulfur (S 0, O 0 or –1) is preferred over all-octet (S +2, O –1).

notes.heading: Sigma and pi bonds
points: Sigma: head-on overlap, electron density along the bond axis. Pi: sideways overlap of p orbitals, density above and below the axis.
Single bond = one σ; double = one σ + one π; triple = one σ + two π.
Pi bonds are generally weaker than sigma, so C=C (614) is less than double C–C (346).
Count σ and π from the structure: every bond has one σ; each extra bond is a π.

notes.heading: Hybridization
points: Hybridization is mixing atomic orbitals to form new hybrid orbitals for bonding; the number of hybrids equals the number mixed.
sp³: 4 domains, tetrahedral, 109.5°. sp²: 3 domains, trigonal planar, 120°. sp: 2 domains, linear, 180°.
Unhybridized p orbitals form pi bonds: one left in sp², two in sp.
Number of hybrid orbitals equals number of electron domains; multiple bonds count as one domain.
Examples: C in CH₄ sp³, ethene sp², ethyne sp; O in H₂O sp³; benzene carbons sp².

definitions.definition: Electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the positively charged nuclei of the two bonded atoms.
definitions.trap: Do not say it is attraction between atoms or only 'sharing electrons'.

definitions.definition: The tendency of atoms to gain a valence shell containing a total of eight electrons, usually by bonding.
definitions.trap: It is a rule of thumb with exceptions, not a law.

definitions.definition: A diagram showing all valence electrons of a covalent species, bonding and non-bonding pairs, as dots, crosses or dashes.
definitions.trap: Do not show inner-shell electrons.

definitions.definition: The number of bonded electron pairs between two atoms.
definitions.trap: Delocalized bonds have fractional order, e.g. 1.5 in ozone.

definitions.definition: A covalent bond in which both shared electrons come from the same atom.
definitions.trap: Not a different bond type once formed; it is identical to other covalent bonds.

definitions.definition: An atom or group with a lone pair of electrons that forms a coordination bond to a central metal ion.
definitions.trap: A ligand donates the pair; the metal ion accepts it.

definitions.definition: A region of high electron density around a central atom: a lone pair, a single bond, or a double or triple bond.
definitions.trap: A double or triple bond counts as one domain, not two or three.

definitions.definition: Predicts molecular shape because electron domains around a central atom repel and arrange themselves as far apart as possible.
definitions.trap: Lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, so angles shrink.

definitions.definition: The angle between bonding pairs, that is between two bonds, at a central atom.
definitions.trap: Quote reduced values with lone pairs, e.g. 107° for NH₃, not 109.5°.

definitions.definition: The attraction of an atom for the bonding pair of electrons in a covalent bond.
definitions.trap: Do not confuse with ionization energy or electron affinity, or mention gaseous atoms.

definitions.definition: Unequal sharing of the bonding pair, arising from the difference in electronegativity of the bonded atoms.
definitions.trap: Identical atoms give a non-polar bond.

definitions.definition: The separation of charge between non-identical bonded atoms, or across a molecule, shown as a vector towards the more electronegative atom.
definitions.trap: Arrow points to the more electronegative atom, not the less.

definitions.definition: A molecule whose bond dipoles do not cancel, giving a net dipole with partial negative and positive ends.
definitions.trap: Polar bonds alone do not make a polar molecule (CO₂, BF₃).

definitions.definition: A giant continuous three-dimensional lattice of atoms joined by covalent bonds.
definitions.trap: It is not made of molecules, so no intermolecular forces are broken on melting.

definitions.definition: Different structural forms of the same element, with different chemical and physical properties.
definitions.trap: Say structural forms of an element, not different elements.

definitions.definition: Weak electrostatic forces of attraction between molecules, weaker than covalent bonds.
definitions.trap: Breaking them on boiling does not break covalent bonds inside molecules.

definitions.definition: Intermolecular forces from temporary instantaneous dipoles in one molecule inducing dipoles in neighbouring molecules.
definitions.trap: Present in all molecules; strength rises with more electrons, not just mass.

definitions.definition: Attractions between the permanent dipoles of neighbouring polar molecules.
definitions.trap: Not present in non-polar molecules such as CO₂.

definitions.definition: Attraction between a hydrogen covalently bonded to F, O or N and a lone pair on another electronegative atom.
must_say: hydrogen bonded to F, O or N
definitions.trap: It is an intermolecular force, not a covalent bond; H must be bonded directly to N, O or F.

definitions.definition: Inclusive term for London (dispersion), dipole–induced dipole and dipole–dipole forces.
definitions.trap: Do not include hydrogen bonding.

definitions.definition: Technique separating mixture components by their different attractions, through intermolecular forces, to a mobile phase and a stationary phase.
definitions.trap: Separation is by relative affinity, not by mass alone.

definitions.definition: Distance travelled by the spot divided by the distance travelled by the solvent front.
definitions.trap: Measure from the baseline; the value has no units and lies between 0 and 1.

definitions.definition: Alternative Lewis formulas differing in the position of double bonds, which together represent one molecule.
definitions.trap: The molecule does not switch between them; it is a hybrid.

definitions.definition: Sharing of electrons across more than two atoms, rather than being localized between one pair of atoms.
definitions.trap: Not just 'electrons moving freely'; they are spread over several bonds.

definitions.definition: A central atom with more than eight valence electrons, having five or six electron pairs around it.
definitions.trap: Only applies to larger central atoms, not period 2 elements such as carbon or nitrogen.

definitions.definition: The charge an atom would have if bonding electrons were shared equally and its non-bonding electrons were not shared at all.
definitions.trap: Formula is VE – (NBE + ½BE); do not forget the half on bonding electrons.

definitions.definition: A bond formed by head-on overlap of atomic orbitals, with electron density concentrated along the bond axis.
definitions.trap: Single bonds are always sigma; do not call it sideways overlap.

definitions.definition: A bond formed by lateral overlap of p orbitals, with electron density on opposite sides of the bond axis.
definitions.trap: Pi bonds are only in multiple bonds, alongside a sigma bond.

definitions.definition: The mixing of atomic orbitals to form new hybrid orbitals for bonding.
definitions.trap: It is not just promotion of electrons, nor simply overlapping of orbitals.

definitions.definition: The average distance between two bonded nuclei.
definitions.trap: Say nuclei, not atoms' surfaces or electrons.
